transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-18
Start: 15:32 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes (recording)
Attendees: Priya Mehta (Redwood AE), Ethan Wu (Redwood SE), Aria Gomez (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Nimbus Head of Platform), Carlos Ruiz (Nimbus Network Eng), Jenna Li (Nimbus ML Infra Lead), Ravi Singh (CISO)

---
[00:00:00] Priya: All right, team, thanks for carving time. Quick context: Redwood + Nimbus pilot, focus on private VPC deployment and making sure inference meets the interactive 150ms tail latency target under our typical load. Ethan will drive the runtime bits and I'll walk networking.

[00:00:18] Maya: Awesome. We have the platform folks and net team here. Primary ask is to avoid public egress where possible, preserve data residency, and keep latency under 200ms 95th for our chat endpoint.

[00:00:34] Carlos: Quick note, our current VPC has two availability-zone subnets, one NAT gw per AZ, and a few cross-account PrivateLink endpoints already used for third-party logging. We want to understand whether Redwood Private needs extra ENIs or if we can reuse existing endpoints.

[00:00:50] Ethan: Great, thanks Carlos. At a high level, Redwood Private can be deployed in your VPC using either PrivateLink endpoints for control-plane traffic and model fetches, or we can allow egress through NAT for model downloads and telemetry. For inference, the local serving runtime sits inside your network so tokens don't cross public internet. PrivateLink tends to be more deterministic for latency but has nuances with DNS and TLS SNI.

[00:01:17] Jenna: Can you explain the DNS nuance? We run a split-horizon resolver (in- VPC route 53 resolver) and some of our internal names are conditional.

[00:01:28] Ethan: Yes. Two common patterns: 1) Use a VPC Resolver outbound endpoint with conditional forwarding to the Redwood control plane private zone; or 2) configure your AWS PrivateLink endpoint to register private hosted zones and use resolver rules. In practice, we sometimes see TTLs cause unresolved name issues for the first few requests — that's perceived as cold-start DNS blips.

[00:01:48] Carlos: We also hit MTU fragmentation when we did GPU-instances with ENI secondary interfaces before — packets >1500 get weird. Any recommendations?

[00:01:58] Aria: MTU is real. We recommend checking jumbo frame settings between ENIs and any NAT/Transit gateway. For model payloads and KV cache snapshots we occasionally push ~1.2MB blobs; if your MTU is 1500 and you have an extra encapsulation (like ENA or transit), fragmentation can cause retries and spike latency. We prefer path MTU discovery plus explicitly set the ENI MTU to 9001 where possible for intra-cluster traffic.

[00:02:23] Maya: Is enabling jumbo frames an org-wide change? We've got a lot of managed services that assume 1500.

[00:02:31] Priya: It's not required for functionality, but it's an optimization. For the pilot, we can recommend isolating the Redwood fleet into subnets where jumbo is enabled at the AZ level and keep cross-team managed services on 1500 to avoid broad changes.

[00:02:44] Ravi (CISO): Security question — how do audit logs and KMS access work when using PrivateLink? We need proof that keys never leave our account.

[00:02:54] Ethan: Good point. With Redwood Private in-VPC, keys for disk encryption and KMS are in your account — we integrate with customer KMS via role assumption; nothing leaves your account. For control plane telemetry that flows to Redwood, we can route via PrivateLink and set up flow logs + VPC endpoint policies. We will provide the PrivateLink policy templates.

[00:03:15] Carlos: About source/dest checks on ENIs — if we create a shared appliance model (like an inference pool across AZs), do we need to disable source/dest checks?

[00:03:26] Aria: If you're NAT-ing through an appliance or using a transit gateway with source NAT, some instances will need source/dest disabled. For our managed pool, we often put a small NAT per subnet and keep source/dest check enabled on the inference instances, that simplifies security groups. But if you do asymmetric routing via firewall appliances, you will need to disable and handle route tables carefully.

[00:03:48] Maya: Okay. Shifting to runtime: Jenna, any latency budgets on batching or cold-start?

[00:03:56] Jenna: We're targeting 95th < 200ms and p99 < 400ms for interactive queries at 10 qps. Cold-starts are our biggest pain, especially with KV cache misses and first-token decoding.

[00:04:06] Ethan: On the runtime side, two levers are critical: KV cache warmup and dynamic batching. KV cache warmup: we preload common prefix tokens into the cache; that reduces repeated KV fetches to disk or remote object store. In Redwood's runtime we have an option to prefetch top-N recent prefixes or to keep a persistent in-memory shard pinned to GPU memory. The tradeoff is RAM/GPU foot print versus cold-start latency.

[00:04:30] Priya: Also quantization: Nimbus mentioned wanting to squeeze cost. For your model family, the SE team ran an int8 pass that reduced token cost by ~2.3x but added a small drop in semantic recall in a few edge prompts. We'll share the eval matrix.

[00:04:47] Jenna: We care about hallucination rates. How painful is rolling back quantization if we see semantic regressions?

[00:04:52] Ethan: We support side-by-side model variants. You can do canary traffic to FP16 while most traffic hits int8, and automatic fallback to FP16 on regression triggers. The runtime supports per-route model pins so you can route sensitive flows to the higher-precision model.

[00:05:07] Carlos: Back to network: is there any hairpinning when you talk to PrivateLink endpoints from instances that also host customers' egress? We've observed connection burn when clients call an endpoint that maps back to the same AZ.

[00:05:19] Aria: Hairpin NAT can happen when the ENI IP range overlaps or when using proxying appliances without proper SNAT. Our suggestion: use separate subnets for control plane vs data plane. Ensure endpoint network interfaces are in private subnets and route table priorities prefer local ENIs. Also, disable source/dest where appropriate. This reduces connection churn.

[00:05:41] Maya: Do we need to open any special ports? We're locked down to a small ephemeral port range and strictly defined SGs.

[00:05:47] Priya: For inference: outbound to the PrivateLink endpoint over TLS (443) for control/config; data plane between runtime nodes uses gRPC (configurable ports) and we can pin it to a narrow range. We'll provide the exact port list.

[00:05:59] Ravi: How about certs and SNI? We require mTLS between services for internal apps. Does Redwood support mTLS?

[00:06:06] Ethan: Yes, we support mTLS for control-plane and can integrate with your internal PKI — we can accept client certs at the PrivateLink endpoint and verify them with your CA. We typically sign server certs ourselves but for high-security customers we swap to customer CA-signed certs.

[00:06:21] Carlos: On telemetry, if we route metrics through PrivateLink, do we risk adding tail latency to inference because of blocking synchronous telemetry calls?

[00:06:29] Aria: We recommend async fire-and-forget telemetry over a dedicated channel; don't block the token path. Redwood can buffer metrics locally and push to your telemetry collector in batches. The runtime will only block on critical control plane calls (rollouts, model fetch) which we instrument separately.

[00:06:45] Maya: Let's talk numbers. Under our test load we need 10 qps sustained with 80 token average per request. What's the expected throughput and cost on a 4xA10 pool?

[00:06:56] Ethan: Rough ballpark: a single 4x A10 serving group, with batching tuned to 8-12 tokens per batch and KV cache warm, should handle ~25-40 qps depending on prompt complexity. For your 10 qps target it's comfortably within saturation, but the tail latency depends on batching window. If you set max latency window to 50ms for batching we maintain interactive latencies but give up some throughput efficiency.

[00:07:17] Jenna: Is there automatic batching tuning? We don't want to manually tune windows for every route.

[00:07:22] Ethan: Redwood Optimize can suggest batching policies based on observed inter-arrival times. For pilots, we can start with a conservative policy (max wait 30-50ms, max tokens per batch 12) and the system will emit cost/latency tradeoffs in the console.

[00:07:35] Maya: How about cold network paths — e.g., if a scale event pulls new nodes from a private AMI that needs to pull a 600MB model blob. Does that hit our NAT and cause egress bursts?

[00:07:47] Priya: Yes, model pulls can cause egress bursts. Two mitigations: 1) Pre-stage models in a shared EFS or local cache in your account so new instances pull locally; 2) use an S3 VPC endpoint or PrivateLink for artifact distribution. We'll provide recommendations and a script to seed images and model shards to reduce NAT egress.

[00:08:05] Carlos: About flow logs and troubleshooting, what logs should we expect from Redwood agents?

[00:08:11] Ethan: We'll emit per-route request logs (masked content), KV cache hit/miss metrics, batching windows, and network-level connection metrics. These can be pushed to your CloudWatch/Datadog via PrivateLink endpoints. We'll share the mapping of log names.

[00:08:24] Speaker 1: (inaudible) some missed tokens — I think that was a transcription hiccup.

[00:08:30] Jenna: Did you mention the KV cache warmup strategy that trades memory for latency? Can you quantify?

[00:08:36] Ethan: Sure. Example: for a 10M-token working set, keeping a top-100k prefix cache in-memory can reduce median latency for repeat prefixes by 30-60ms. That cache may consume X GiB of host RAM (we'll share exact numbers per model). Alternatively, persistent on-disk shards with async prefetch reduce memory pressure but add a 50-120ms hit on first token.

[00:08:56] Priya: For the pilot we recommend pinning a small in-memory cache + async filesystem-backed second tier. That balances memory and predictable latency.

[00:09:05] Maya: What about quantization rollbacks — do we have automatic fallback if quality drops? You mentioned canary, but can that be automated?

[00:09:12] Ethan: Yes, you can wire in eval triggers. Redwood Optimize can run prompt sets against both variants and trigger an automatic rollback to FP16 if a quality metric falls below threshold. This is usually configured as a policy: e.g., rollback if semantic similarity delta > 0.05 on critical prompts.

[00:09:29] Carlos: One operational gotcha we hit earlier: our NAT gateway hit source port exhaustion during heavy model downloads. Any mitigations?

[00:09:36] Aria: Source port exhaustion is common when many short TCP connections are used. Mitigations: enable long-lived connections, reuse HTTP keepalive to the S3/PrivateLink endpoint, or multiplex model download streams. Also consider additional NAT gw's per AZ or use a gateway load balancer to distribute.

[00:09:52] Priya: For downloads we provide an S3 signed URL pattern and recommend pre-warming the artifact cache with long-live TCP sessions. We'll share a prewarm script.

[00:10:02] Maya: Good. Any other networking pitfalls?

[00:10:06] Carlos: What about cross-account PrivateLink? We use multiple AWS accounts; will Redwood's endpoint support cross-account access?

[00:10:12] Ethan: Yes, PrivateLink supports cross-account endpoints with an explicit endpoint service permissions list on our side. You'll need to accept the endpoint connection and we'll provide the service name and the policy. Be mindful of route table propagation across shared services.

[00:10:24] Ravi: I want to reiterate we need to verify key custody and support an audit run before any production run.

[00:10:30] Priya: Understood. We'll send our security pack and KMS integration docs. We'll also propose a short audit plan for your team and Redwood security to run together.

[00:10:38] Maya: Wrap up — we need a short pilot checklist, the exact ports/SGs, PrivateLink policy templates, model prewarm script, and a suggested batching profile. Who's owning those?

[00:10:48] Priya: Redwood: I'll own checklist and policy templates, Ethan will own prewarm script and batching profile. Nimbus: Carlos and Jenna will share their subnet CIDRs and flow logs.

[00:10:58] Ethan: We'll also run a quick KV-cache warmup benchmark on a sample of Nimbus prompts and return the numbers. Expect that by next week.

[00:11:05] Maya: Great. Any last Qs?

[00:11:08] Jenna: One small item: do you support sidecar proxies or do you require direct connectivity? We use Envoy as a policy enforcement point.

[00:11:14] Aria: We support Envoy sidecars; Redwood's runtime has a documented integration pattern. We recommend L7 routing at the sidecar and L4 for the runtime to minimize overhead.

[00:11:24] Priya: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts.

[00:11:28] (Recording continues with light Q/A and background chatter until 00:62:00)
